b063d0666d88: Jak AA rozrosło się z dwóch osób?
9f6d2121ca4c: Wychodząc do ludzi i szukając kolejnych alkoholików. Gdy Bill W. i dr Bob spotkali się w Akron w 1935 roku, zadzwonili razem do szpitala i poprosili o kandydata (s. 156). Ten człowiek stał się trzecim członkiem, a we trzech poszli szukać czwartego (s. 158).
d8f37104e469: Każdy, kto wyzdrowiał, robił to samo dla następnego. Wielka Księga, napisana w 1939 roku, opisuje około stu osób, do których dotarto w ten sposób (s. xiii).
7a6ca76656f1: Dr Bob, przemawiając w 1948 roku, opisał to tak samo: „Natychmiast zaczęliśmy rozglądać się za kandydatami”.
bc48c35c84dc: Nie było żadnej reklamy ani programu, do którego można by się zapisać. Wspólnota była tym, co wyrosło wokół ludzi ratujących pijaków.
0033a6a1467b: Rozdział 11, „Wizja dla ciebie”, opowiada tę historię bez nazwisk; przypisy dodane w późniejszych wydaniach mówią, kim byli ci ludzie.
323838d8bd45: <0>Jeden człowiek, samotny i roztrzęsiony.</0> W 1935 roku człowiek trzeźwy „zaledwie od kilku miesięcy” (s. 154) utknął w obcym mieście po niepowodzeniu w interesach. Kuszony przez hotelowy bar, pomyślał o „tamtych innych alkoholikach” (s. 154) i zadzwonił do duchownego, żeby jakiegoś znaleźć (s. 154–155). To doprowadziło go do dr. Boba (przypis na s. 155).
0dd1a2e6b7f2: <0>Drugi.</0> Dr Bob miał jeszcze jeden ciąg, potem wyruszył stanąć przed ludźmi, których się bał, i od tamtej pory nie wypił ani kieliszka (s. 155–156).
a90f522c73b6: <0>Trzeci, znaleziony celowo.</0> „Obaj zobaczyli, że muszą pozostać aktywni duchowo” (s. 156). Zadzwonili do przełożonej pielęgniarek w szpitalu i poprosili o „pierwszorzędnego kandydata alkoholika” (s. 156): był to prawnik, który trafiał tam osiem razy w ciągu sześciu miesięcy i był przypięty pasami do łóżka. Trzeciego dnia powierzył swoje życie opiece Boga; w czerwcu 1935 roku wyszedł stamtąd jako wolny człowiek i nigdy więcej nie pił (s. 158).
0e657d4a7afb: <0>Czwarty.</0> „Jak więc widzisz, w tamtym mieście było trzech alkoholików, którzy czuli teraz, że muszą dać innym to, co sami znaleźli, albo przepadną” (s. 158). „Po kilku nieudanych próbach znalezienia innych pojawił się czwarty” (s. 158).
1f02dbe796c5: <0>Potem kolejni.</0> „Półtora roku później tym trzem udało się z siedmioma kolejnymi” (s. 159). Zaczęli spotykać się raz w tygodniu wieczorem, żeby nowi ludzie mieli czas i miejsce, gdzie mogą przynieść swoje problemy (s. 159–160). Do 1939 roku na mityng w Akron przychodziło „zazwyczaj sześćdziesiąt lub osiemdziesiąt osób” (s. 161), a coś podobnego działo się w pewnym mieście na wschodzie i w „małych gromadkach po dwie, trzy i pięć osób” gdzie indziej (s. 162).
6f2d4ea34681: Książka zakładała, że będzie to trwało w ten sam sposób: czytelnicy „będą docierać do kolejnych chorych” (s. 153), a jeden członek sam w nowym mieście, współpracując z lekarzem i szpitalem, wkrótce będzie miał „przyjaciół bez liku” (s. 163). Przedmowa z 1939 roku liczy „ponad stu mężczyzn i kobiet, którzy wyzdrowieli” (s. xiii).
95ef237adac8: Ostatnie duże przemówienie dr. Boba, wygłoszone w Detroit w grudniu 1948 roku, zostało wydrukowane w „Grapevine” w 1973 roku, a dziś znajduje się w broszurze <0>Współzałożyciele Anonimowych Alkoholików</0> (P-53, s. 9–20).
27d7b4fc568d: Mówi, że przed Akron Bill „nie nawrócił ani jednej osoby, ani jednej” (P-53). On sam robił wszystko, czego wymagała Grupa Oksfordzka, a mimo to co wieczór się upijał. Nie powiedziano mu tylko o tym, co Bill zrobił tamtej niedzieli: „spróbować pomóc komuś innemu” (P-53). Po jego ostatnim kieliszku 10 czerwca 1935 roku: „Natychmiast zaczęliśmy rozglądać się za kandydatami” (P-53). Pierwszym był Bill D., potem „trzech kandydatów spadło nam na głowę niemal jednocześnie” (P-53). Dr Bob rozmawiał z mężczyznami w szpitalnych łóżkach całymi godzinami. Później: „W miarę jak rośliśmy, zaczęły powstawać odgałęzienia, jedno w Cleveland” (P-53).
f8efa5d85942: <0>Przedmowa do drugiego wydania (1955).</0> Po spotkaniu z dr. Bobem obaj mężczyźni „zabrali się niemal gorączkowo do pracy z alkoholikami trafiającymi na oddział Akron City Hospital” (s. xvii). Kiedy Bill jesienią 1935 roku wrócił do Nowego Jorku, „szybko uformowała się” tam druga grupa, a trzecia powstała w Cleveland w 1937 roku (s. xvii); gdy wiosną 1939 roku ukazała się książka, członków było około stu (s. xvii). Potem artykuły w czasopismach przyniosły zalew listów i do końca 1941 roku członków było około 8000 (s. xviii).
3d6650268f9d: <0><1>Anonimowi Alkoholicy wkraczają w dojrzałość</1> (1957).</0> Bill wspomina stronę nowojorską: mityngi w jego salonie na Brooklynie i wyprawy do Calvary Mission i Towns Hospital „w gorączkowym poszukiwaniu kolejnych kandydatów” (<2>Wkraczają w dojrzałość</2>, 1957). W listopadzie 1937 roku on i dr Bob podsumowali wyniki w salonie dr. Boba i wyliczyli, że „ponad czterdziestu alkoholików pozostawało zupełnie trzeźwych” (<3>Wkraczają w dojrzałość</3>, 1957). Uderzył ich łańcuch: „jeden alkoholik niosący dobrą nowinę następnemu” (<4>Wkraczają w dojrzałość</4>, 1957).
c7a3c8e7a399: W najwcześniejszych źródłach punktem wyjścia nie jest wspólnota. Jest nim ratunek. Dwaj mężczyźni musieli znaleźć trzeciego, inaczej nigdy nie byłoby ich więcej niż dwóch, a każdego następnego członka znaleziono w ten sam sposób: pijaka w szpitalu albo w domu, do którego dotarł ktoś, kto wyzdrowiał. Mityngi przyszły później, jako miejsce dla odnajdywanych ludzi. To jest praca, którą opisuje Rozdział 7 (s. 89–103).

9874ea6fe505: Relacja z 1939 roku: Rozdział 11, „Wizja dla ciebie”
211f93e1746e: Pierwsza relacja samej Wielkiej Księgi znajduje się w Rozdziale 11, napisanym w 1939 roku (uwaga na s. 161). Nie wymienia nikogo z nazwiska. Jeden z członków, jak mówi, odbył w 1935 roku podróż służbową do „pewnego zachodniego miasta”, która skończyła się procesem i zostawiła go zniechęconego, niemal bez grosza i samotnego (s. 153–154). Słaby fizycznie i trzeźwy zaledwie od kilku miesięcy, „Tak bardzo chciał z kimś porozmawiać, ale z kim?” (s. 154).
a2afc47dcb82: W hotelowym holu stał między barem na jednym końcu a spisem kościołów na drugim (s. 154). Kusiło go, żeby usiąść w barze z piwem imbirowym, a potem dostrzegł niebezpieczeństwo: „Znów było to stare, podstępne szaleństwo – ten pierwszy kieliszek”. (s. 154). Zawrócić pomogła mu myśl o rodzinie i o „ludziach, którzy umrą, bo nie będą wiedzieć, jak wyzdrowieć” (s. 154). „Wybrawszy na chybił trafił kościół ze spisu, wszedł do budki i podniósł słuchawkę”. (s. 155).
07e5080a8348: Telefon do duchownego doprowadził go do miejscowego człowieka, kiedyś zdolnego i szanowanego, teraz bliskiego dna (s. 155). Przypis w dzisiejszym wydaniu mówi, że była to pierwsza wizyta Billa u dr. Boba (s. 155). Ten człowiek zgodził się, że nie przestanie pić siłą woli i że potrzebuje doświadczenia duchowego, ale z początku nie chciał zapłacić ceny, jaką było przyznanie się do picia przed ludźmi, od których zależało jego utrzymanie (s. 155). Zaprosił Billa do swojego domu, poszedł w jeszcze jeden ciąg, a potem obszedł ludzi, których skrzywdził, i powiedział im prawdę (s. 155–156).
89286b1d6749: Relacja samego dr. Boba (jego historia, napisana w 1939 roku)
6cc0797156ff: „Koszmar doktora Boba”, pierwsza historia osobista w książce, została napisana, gdy był trzeźwy od około czterech lat (s. 180). Poszli następnego dnia, a on kazał żonie obiecać, że zostaną piętnaście minut (s. 179). „Weszliśmy do jej domu dokładnie o piątej, a kiedy wychodziliśmy, była jedenasta piętnaście”. (s. 179).
30c2540bb312: Przestał pić na około trzy tygodnie, potem mocno pił na zjeździe lekarzy w Atlantic City; jego nowy przyjaciel przywiózł go do domu, a ostatni kieliszek wypił 10 czerwca 1935 roku (s. 179–180).
c612145b1cd1: Dlaczego tym razem zadziałało, skoro czytanie i rozmowy z ekspertami nie pomogły? Ponieważ był on „pierwszym żywym człowiekiem, z jakim kiedykolwiek rozmawiałem, który wiedział, o czym mówi w sprawie alkoholizmu, z własnego doświadczenia” (s. 180). „Innymi słowy, mówił moim językiem”. (s. 180).
eb368b3148f5: Relacja z 1955 roku: Przedmowa do drugiego wydania
b49ce740609e: Przedmowa z 1955 roku podaje zarys, wciąż bez nazwisk. Makler został uwolniony od obsesji picia około sześciu miesięcy wcześniej, po spotkaniu z przyjacielem alkoholikiem związanym z Grupami Oksfordzkimi (s. xv–xvi). Pracował z wieloma alkoholikami, ale nie doprowadził do trzeźwości żadnego (s. xvi). Utknąwszy w Akron po nieudanym przedsięwzięciu i bojąc się picia, „Nagle zrozumiał, że aby ocalić siebie, musi zanieść swoje posłanie innemu alkoholikowi”. (s. xvi). Przedmowa datuje spotkanie na „czerwiec 1935 roku, podczas rozmowy nowojorskiego maklera giełdowego z lekarzem z Akron” (s. xv).
e1191c74ce95: <0>Dr Bob, 1948.</0> Jego ostatnie duże przemówienie, nagrane w Detroit w grudniu 1948 roku i po raz pierwszy wydrukowane w „Grapevine” w 1973 roku, jest przedrukowane w P-53 (P-53). Wymienia tam hotel Mayflower, mówi, że Bill zobaczył nazwisko pastora Waltera Tunksa na tablicy w holu i zadzwonił do niego, a Tunks dał mu listę dziewięciu czy dziesięciu osób z Grupy Oksfordzkiej (P-53). Pod koniec listy Bill dotarł do Henrietty Seiberling, która zaprosiła go na lunch, a potem zadzwoniła do żony dr. Boba, Anne; ponieważ dr Bob był tego dnia zbyt pijany, przyszli następnego dnia, w niedzielę, w Dzień Matki (P-53). Mówi też, co było dla niego nowe: Grupa Oksfordzka kazała mu czytać, modlić się i chodzić na spotkania, „Ale jedynej rzeczy, której mi nie powiedzieli, była ta jedna rzecz, którą Bill zrobił tamtej niedzieli – spróbować pomóc komuś innemu”. (P-53).
62f248d1f9c6: <0>Bill W., 1957.</0> W <1>Anonimowi Alkoholicy wkraczają w dojrzałość</1> Bill mówi, że w maju 1935 roku pojechał do Akron na walkę o pełnomocnictwa w małej firmie produkującej obrabiarki, przegrał i został w Mayflower z około dziesięcioma dolarami (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Krążąc po holu w przeddzień Dnia Matki, po raz pierwszy zrozumiał, że to pomaganie innym utrzymywało go w trzeźwości: „Potrzebujesz drugiego alkoholika tak samo, jak on potrzebuje ciebie!” (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Wybrał pastora ze spisu kościołów, dostał listę około dziesięciu nazwisk i dotarł do Henrietty Seiberling w domku przy bramie posiadłości Seiberlingów (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Dr Bob i Anne przyszli następnego popołudnia o piątej, a obaj mężczyźni rozmawiali sami do jedenastej (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill mówi, że posłuchał rady doktora Silkwortha, by przestać kazać i mówić o faktach medycznych i własnym przypadku, i że rozmowa była obopólna: „Wiedziałem, że potrzebuję tego alkoholika tak samo, jak on potrzebował mnie”. (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
9d42951c157b: <0>Miesiąc.</0> Przedmowa z 1955 roku mówi o czerwcu 1935 roku (s. xv). Historia dr. Boba z 1939 roku umieszcza spotkanie w Dniu Matki, co najmniej trzy tygodnie przed jego ostatnim kieliszkiem 10 czerwca (s. 179–180), a biografie w P-53 (broszura © 2017) i <1>Wkraczają w dojrzałość</1> (1957) mówią o maju 1935 roku. The method, in the book's order: - <0>Put it on paper.</0> List the people, institutions or principles you're angry with (p. 64). - <1>Ask why.</1> Usually it was found that self-esteem, pocketbook, ambitions or personal relationships, including sex, were "hurt or threatened" (pp. 64–65). - <2>Set the injury opposite each name.</2> The book's example (p. 65) has three columns: "I'm resentful at," "The Cause," and "Affects my." The word "fear" is written in beside several of the entries. - <3>Go back through your whole life.</3> "Nothing counted but thoroughness and honesty" (p. 65). - <4>Then look at it differently.</4> The book says concluding that others were wrong was as far as most people got, and it kept them sore (p. 66). Resentment, for the alcoholic, is fatal: it shuts us off "from the sunlight of the Spirit" (p. 66). So they came to see the people who wronged them as perhaps spiritually sick, and asked God to help them show those people the patience they'd give a sick friend (pp. 66–67). - <5>Find your own part.</5> Putting aside the other person's wrongs, they looked for their own mistakes: "Where had we been selfish, dishonest, self-seeking and frightened?" (p. 67) Even where it wasn't entirely their fault, they tried to disregard the other person. "The inventory was ours, not the other man's" (p. 67). They listed their faults in black and white (p. 67).

Facing a possible criminal offence or a debt that could cost a job, members asked for strength to do the right thing "no matter what the personal consequences may be" (p. 79): "We may lose our position or reputation or face jail, but we are willing" (p. 79).
98a20a41bf67: But other people are usually involved, so "we are not to be the hasty and foolish martyr" (p. 79) who sacrifices others to save himself. Its example: a man owed alimony and faced arrest. Walking into court would have been heroic, but in jail he could support neither family. So he wrote to his first wife, admitted his faults, sent a little money, and said he'd go to jail if she insisted (p. 79). The rule the book draws: "Before taking drastic action which might implicate other people we secure their consent" (p. 80). Then, if the drastic step is still called for, "we must not shrink" (p. 80). Another member, after consulting his wife and partner, cleared a rival he'd ruined by standing up in church and explaining (p. 80).

15c435d3802b: No, and no. The 1939 text asks for an admission made "to our innermost selves" (p. 30), not out loud at a meeting, and it describes no way of introducing yourself.
e873cfdea838: Bill W. wrote in 1946 that in most groups a newcomer "doesn't even have to admit he is an alcoholic" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). He can join on the suspicion that he may be one.
f0f074c07db8: The introduction "My name is ___, and I'm an alcoholic" turns up in the Big Book only in a few personal stories in Parts II and III of the fourth edition (2001), not in the 1939 text. <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) says Bill probably picked the custom up from the Oxford Group, and P-43 says groups differ in how it's done.
a940ef45a982: The book is firm about one thing: nobody should label another person an alcoholic. "Let him draw his own conclusion." (p. 92).
bec2de4a01c2: <0>An inner admission.</0> "We learned that we had to fully concede to our innermost selves that we were alcoholics." (p. 30). The book calls this the first step in recovery, and the concession is to oneself.
b8b9d4c426db: <0>Self-diagnosis.</0> "We do not like to pronounce any individual as alcoholic, but you can quickly diagnose yourself." (p. 31). See <1>How do I know if I'm an alcoholic?</1>
19410316f084: <0>No labeling by others.</0> When talking with a prospect, the member describes himself as an alcoholic (p. 91) but is told to "be careful not to brand him as an alcoholic" (p. 92). If the man insists he can still control his drinking, "tell him that possibly he can—if he is not too alcoholic" (p. 92).
d5d5b45c956b: <0>Step One</0> says "We admitted we were powerless over alcohol—that our lives had become unmanageable." (p. 59). The Step doesn't say to whom; Chapter 3's description of "the first step in recovery" (p. 30) is a concession to oneself.
93ed86af71be: Nowhere in pages 1–164 does the book describe members introducing themselves at a meeting, or require anyone to say anything there.
e367719e458c: The Long Form of Tradition Three says A.A.'s membership "ought to include all who suffer from alcoholism" (p. 563); the later short form (by 1950) asks only for a desire to stop drinking (p. 562). Neither asks for an admission. Bill's 1946 essay goes further: "Nowadays, in most groups, he doesn't even have to admit he is an alcoholic." (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). He can join "on the mere suspicion that he may be one" (same essay).
be5d68ee0106: <0>Personal stories in the fourth edition.</0> A search of the whole fourth-edition text finds the meeting introduction only in a few stories in Parts II and III, the sections that hold later members' stories: a newcomer who, because everyone around the table was saying they were alcoholics, said his name and "Hi, I'm an alcoholic" (p. 401); a "big clown" at a meeting shouting "My name is Frank, and I'm an alcoholic" (p. 414); a woman who, at her first meeting on her own, said "I am an alcoholic" after years of saying "I'm with him" at her father's meetings (p. 515). These are members' own experience, not the program text.
1462afaf0c8e: <0><1>Pass It On</1> (1984)</0> lists it among early customs: members introduced themselves with "My name is Bill W. I'm an alcoholic." (<2>Pass It On</2>, 1984). Bill probably got it from the Oxford Group meetings of the mid-1930s, where members in a circle said "My name is so-and-so" to identify themselves.
b69f8a24cf34: <0>P-43</0> (<1>The Twelve Traditions Illustrated</1>, © 1971, this printing updated 2023), on Tradition Four: in one part of the U.S. a speaker who begins "My name is Ann, and I am an alcoholic" gets respectful silence; in another everybody shouts "Hi, Ann!"; elsewhere she may use her full name. "In each neighborhood in every part of the world reached by A.A., the local group is free to work out its own customs." (P-43).
a06d75bc132e: Saying "I'm an alcoholic" at a meeting is a custom, with roots in the Oxford Group, that varies from place to place. The Big Book asks for something different and more private: an honest admission to yourself, reached by your own conclusion. A.A.'s membership statement asks only for a desire to stop drinking, and Bill's 1946 essay says that in most groups even the admission isn't required to join.

6ab64df726ca: "Lack of power, that was our dilemma": what dilemma?
ecd8552f7780: The line is on page 45 of the Big Book, near the start of Chapter 4, "We Agnostics." The dilemma is set out in the sentences just before it: moral codes, better philosophies of life and willpower didn't save the writers from alcoholism, because "the needed power wasn't there" (p. 45).
3d331e990708: The next sentence names what they needed: "We had to find a power by which we could live, and it had to be a Power greater than ourselves." (p. 45)
cd7abfff1916: Then the book says what it's for. Its "main object is to enable you to find a Power greater than yourself which will solve your problem" (p. 45).
d92c3fad4e1f: So context confirms the usual reading and sharpens it. The lack was of power to live by what they already knew and wanted, and the line is the point where the book states its own purpose.
286eecee7604: Chapter 4 opens by saying that a reader who can't quit, or can't control the amount once he starts, is probably alcoholic and "may be suffering from an illness which only a spiritual experience will conquer" (p. 44). About half the original fellowship thought they were atheists or agnostics, and they faced the same choice: "To be doomed to an alcoholic death or to live on a spiritual basis are not always easy alternatives to face." (p. 44)
fbf1c43ef728: Then the dilemma, in order (pp. 44–45): 1. <0>Codes weren't enough.</0> "If a mere code of morals or a better philosophy of life were sufficient to overcome alcoholism, many of us would have recovered long ago." (p. 44) 2. <1>Wanting wasn't enough.</1> They could wish to be moral, wish to be comforted by philosophy, even will these things with all their might, "but the needed power wasn't there" (p. 45). 3. <2>Will wasn't enough.</2> "Our human resources, as marshalled by the will, were not sufficient; they failed utterly." (p. 45) 4. <3>The line.</3> "Lack of power, that was our dilemma." (p. 45) 5. <4>The answer and the question.</4> They had to find a Power greater than themselves. "Obviously. But where and how were we to find this Power?" (p. 45) 6. <5>The book's purpose.</5> "Well, that's exactly what this book is about." (p. 45) It means the book is spiritual as well as moral, and "that we are going to talk about God" (p. 45).
abc9b6e0595b: The rest of the page is about what happens next with an agnostic newcomer: his hope rises while the alcoholic problem is explained, and his face falls when God is mentioned (p. 45). The chapter is written for him.
9a312216d208: Chapter 2 uses the same word for the businessman a famous psychiatrist called hopeless. His knowledge of his own mind didn't keep him sober, and his religious convictions, the doctor said, weren't the "vital spiritual experience" he needed (pp. 26–27). "Here was the terrible dilemma in which our friend found himself" (p. 28). It's the same shape: what he had wasn't enough, and the way out was a spiritual experience.

What page 45 describes is the failure of morals, philosophy and will to overcome alcoholism, looking forward to finding "a power by which we could live" (p. 45). 6ad2a522c191: The same paragraph goes straight to action: ask God each morning "what you can do each day for the man who is still sick" (p. 164), and get your own house in order, because "obviously you cannot transmit something you haven't got" (p. 164). b6f1768f235a: The last pages of Chapter 11 picture a reader alone: - "Some day we hope that every alcoholic who journeys will find a Fellowship of Alcoholics Anonymous at his destination." (p. 163) - The reader thinks he's jittery and alone and couldn't do it. 725903159c19: <0>The first</0> (p. 164) sets the book's limits and then gives the reader a daily task: - The book is "suggestive only," and the writers "know only a little" (p. 164). - God will show more, to the reader and to the writers. - Ask in morning meditation what you can do each day for the man who is still sick. "The answers will come, if your own house is in order." (p. 164) - You can't pass on what you don't have. "See to it that your relationship with Him is right, and great events will come to pass for you and countless others." (p. 164) "This is the Great Fact for us." (p. 164)
0d7c525d5583: <0>The last</0> (p. 164) is four short instructions and a farewell: 1. "Abandon yourself to God as you understand God." (p. 164) 2. "Admit your faults to Him and to your fellows." (p. 164) 3. "Clear away the wreckage of your past." (p. 164) 4. "Give freely of what you find and join us." (p. 164)
e3a5e31c1f45: "We shall be with you in the Fellowship of the Spirit, and you will surely meet some of us as you trudge the Road of Happy Destiny." (p. 164) "May God bless you and keep you—until then." (p. 164)

What the setting adds is what stands next to it. The very next sentences say the writers know only a little and that more will be shown, so the phrase sits with an admission about the limits of their knowledge. And it's followed within a few lines by the book's most direct sentences, written as instructions. Both are on the page, and the page needs both. 0a62fcac6908: It complicates it. "Suggestive only" and "we know only a little" are true to the book: it claims no final authority and expects more to be learned. 7810bc81831e: Does the Big Book say alcohol is "but a symptom"? Is drinking the real problem?
251054fdf7c1: Yes, on page 64 of Chapter 5: "Our liquor was but a symptom." (p. 64) The next sentence: "So we had to get down to causes and conditions." (p. 64) In place, it explains why the Third Step decision has to be followed at once by the Fourth Step inventory.
2eb2f94f6a83: So in Chapter 5 the book does treat drinking as the visible sign of something underneath, which it names as self (pp. 62, 64).
a452348a8680: But the same book insists that alcoholism has a physical side too. It says "the body of the alcoholic is quite as abnormal as his mind" (p. xxvi), and "any picture of the alcoholic which leaves out this physical factor is incomplete" (p. xxvi). The doctor's remedy is "entire abstinence" (p. xxx).
8f956188a90c: Context complicates the line. Quoted alone as "drinking isn't the real problem," it drops what the rest of the book says: the alcoholic can never drink safely, and even after recovery "We are not cured of alcoholism." (p. 85)
6f5a3e7e1920: The reader has just made the Third Step decision. The book says that decision, however vital, "could have little permanent effect" unless it was followed at once by a hard effort to face and be rid of "the things in ourselves which had been blocking us" (p. 64). Then: "Our liquor was but a symptom." (p. 64) "So we had to get down to causes and conditions." (p. 64) "Therefore, we started upon a personal inventory." (p. 64)
69abc939c665: The causes, in the next paragraph, are "the flaws in our make-up which caused our failure" (p. 64), and the book has already named the root: "Being convinced that self, manifested in various ways, was what had defeated us" (p. 64). Resentment is the first of those manifestations (p. 64).
8454c09269a4: So "but a symptom" is the book's reason for the inventory: stopping drinking isn't the whole job.
41ec4c436e83: The same word, used at another level
f7007325e2e4: The book uses "symptom" in more than one place, and not always for the same thing. - In the Doctor's Opinion, Dr. Silkworth says that all the types of alcoholic he describes "have one symptom in common: they cannot start drinking without developing the phenomenon of craving" (p. xxx). There the symptom is the craving that alcohol sets off in the body. - A few pages after p. 64, the book uses the word for the people we resent. They were perhaps spiritually sick, and "we did not like their symptoms" (p. 67).
7190f75972c2: The physical side the book won't drop
ce5d47215e68: The Big Book opens with a doctor, and with the members agreeing with him: - "In our belief, any picture of the alcoholic which leaves out this physical factor is incomplete." (p. xxvi) - Dr. Silkworth's theory is an allergy: "the phenomenon of craving is limited to this class and never occurs in the average temperate drinker" (p. xxviii). "These allergic types can never safely use alcohol in any form at all" (p. xxviii). - "The only relief we have to suggest is entire abstinence." (p. xxx) - Chapter 2: once the alcoholic takes any alcohol, "something happens, both in the bodily and mental sense" (p. 22), that makes it virtually impossible to stop. - Chapter 3: "We know that no real alcoholic ever recovers control." (p. 30) The illness is progressive, and "Once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic" (p. 33).
db9df5658ab6: And the mind, and beneath it
934fdfe87bb5: The book also says where the main trouble lies. Since the cycle can't start without the first drink, "the main problem of the alcoholic centers in his mind, rather than in his body" (p. 23). Even the doctor writes that unless the alcoholic can experience "an entire psychic change there is very little hope of his recovery" (p. xxix). Chapter 5 goes a level further down, to self (p. 62).
dc1c8e6f1da1: Read together, these pages describe three layers (the grouping is ours, not the book's): a body that can't take alcohol, a mind with no defense against the first drink, and beneath both, the self that the Steps work on. "But a symptom" speaks about the last of these. It doesn't erase the other two.
2ba9506582b9: The book's answer is both. Drinking is what kills the alcoholic: "with us, to drink is to die" (p. 66). He can never safely do it, and he's never cured (p. 85). Drinking is also the sign of something deeper, which the inventory and the Steps go after. And by Step Ten, the book says, the drink problem goes too: "Instead, the problem has been removed." (p. 85) Even then, that holds only "so long as we keep in fit spiritual condition" (p. 85).

67a9f495b98e: Why do some meetings close with the Lord's Prayer?
7ed8be7978d1: The Big Book's program text (pp. 1–164) never mentions the Lord's Prayer, and nothing in our sources say A.A. adopted it as a rule or explains where the custom began.
8b40f13b2098: What our sources do show is that it was already the custom before the Big Book. A member's story and members' recollections describe Akron meetings in the late 1930s, including those in an Oxford Group home, closing with the Lord's Prayer, and early Cleveland meetings did the same.
2894d8ffd2d2: Writing in 1957 about the early 1940s, Bill W. called it one of A.A.'s "favorites," alongside the Prayer of St. Francis, when the Serenity Prayer joined them (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
ceeb13bc55b0: The fourth-edition stories show members experiencing it differently: one found deep meaning in it, and a Jewish member was told by his sponsor he could say something else.
e301de568b78: What the Big Book's main text says
8252d38a19a2: The first 164 pages don't name the Lord's Prayer. They suggest prayer in the member's own words, with sample prayers and the line "Thy will be done" (pp. 67, 88), and they say members who aren't in a religious body sometimes "select and memorize a few set prayers" (p. 87). The book doesn't say which prayer, if any, should open or close a meeting.
4b0912f36448: The earliest pictures of the custom
e2c86776a56d: These come from members' memories and stories written down later, so they show the practice but not its origin. - <0>Akron, 1937.</0> "He Sold Himself Short," a story in Part I, describes the writer's first meeting in Akron in 1937, before the book: eight or nine alcoholics and their wives, no literature but religious pamphlets, and "The meeting lasted an hour and closed with the Lord's Prayer." (p. 262). - <1>Akron, at T. Henry Williams's house.</1> Until late 1939 the Akron members met in the home of T. Henry and Clarace Williams, who were Oxford Group members (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957; Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). Wally G., an early member, remembered: "After the meeting closed with the Lord's Prayer, all the men beat it to the kitchen for coffee" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). Bob E. remembered that Dr. Bob and T. Henry "teamed" the meeting, and that T. Henry, the Oxford Group host, "took care of the prayers with which the meeting was opened and closed" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). - <2>Cleveland, from 1939.</2> Clarence S., one of the founders of the Cleveland group, described its meetings: "We opened with an audible prayer," then a 45-minute speaker, "and we closed with the Lord's Prayer." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). - <3>Youngstown.</3> A member remembered an early meeting there of four people, two men and two women, who talked a little about the Oxford Group and about Dr. Bob and Bill: "They were using the Lord's Prayer." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). - <4>Akron parties.</4> At the New Year's Eve dance, members gathered around Dr. Bob at midnight; he would say a few words, "and they'd have the Lord's Prayer" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).
be2f9f50103f: So the books place the custom in the Oxford Group years in Akron and carry it into the first meetings that broke away. At T. Henry's house the closing prayer was led by the Oxford Group host, but none of the books says who started the Lord's Prayer custom or why. It would be easy to guess that it came from the Oxford Group or from the members' churches, but our sources don't say so, and this page doesn't either.
8046d5bca5e6: In <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, Bill mentions it twice. He remembers a bilingual meeting in Montreal "where I first heard the Lord's Prayer in French" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). And writing about the Serenity Prayer's spread in the early 1940s, he says it "took its place alongside our two other favorites, the Lord's Prayer and the Prayer of St. Francis" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). That shows how common it was by then; it doesn't explain the origin. (The same book prints a talk by Father Ed Dowling that mentions the Lord's Prayer, but as part of his reflection on Christianity, not about meetings: A.A. Comes of Age, 1957.)

fd2559a2ab4a: Where is "love and tolerance of others is our code"?
ec194e45e258: The line is on page 84 of the Big Book, in Chapter 6, "Into Action." It ends the book's paragraph on Step Ten: "Love and tolerance of others is our code." (p. 84)
0b47a206faa1: Just before it, that paragraph gives Step Ten's daily practice: watch for selfishness, dishonesty, resentment and fear, ask God to remove them, talk them over with someone, make amends quickly, and "Then we resolutely turn our thoughts to someone we can help." (p. 84)
8e43f20f245d: Read in place, the line means what it is usually taken to mean, a code for how we treat other people. The context adds where it sits: it's the way of living that the Step Ten work leads into, not a slogan standing on its own.
977ebb3c5e7b: The book's other uses of "tolerance" show what it has in mind: treating people who wrong us as sick (pp. 67, 70), keeping talk about each other kind (p. 125), and showing no hatred of drinking as an institution (p. 103).
47ada7b8b933: Page 84 opens with the end of the Promises, then turns to Step Ten, which suggests we keep taking personal inventory and set right new mistakes as we go (p. 84). The paragraph says the reader has begun a new way of living by cleaning up the past: "We have entered the world of the Spirit." (p. 84) Growth from here "should continue for our lifetime" (p. 84).
ed70eb462844: Then come the instructions, in order (p. 84): 1. Watch for selfishness, dishonesty, resentment and fear. 2. When they show up, ask God at once to remove them. 3. Talk them over with someone immediately. 4. Make amends quickly if we have harmed anyone. 5. Turn our thoughts to someone we can help.
2e8fa4765729: The paragraph closes on the code. The next paragraph begins "And we have ceased fighting anything or anyone—even alcohol." (p. 84), and goes on to the problem of drink being removed, which holds "so long as we keep in fit spiritual condition" (p. 85).
3ae7eae58e24: So the code sits between the daily inventory and the book's description of a sober life without the fight. It's the last of a run of actions, all pointing away from self: catch the defect, hand it to God, tell someone, repair the harm, help another person, and treat others with love and tolerance.
5264871f2047: What "tolerance" means in the Big Book
de3689994624: The word comes up often, and nearly always about people: - <0>People who have wronged us.</0> In the resentment inventory, the writers saw that the people who hurt them were sick too, and asked God to help them show those people "the same tolerance, pity, and patience that we would cheerfully grant a sick friend" (p. 67). Finishing the inventory, "We have begun to learn tolerance, patience and good will toward all men, even our enemies" (p. 70). - <1>The family.</1> In the amends at home, the recovering man asks each morning that "our Creator show us the way of patience, tolerance, kindliness and love" (p. 83). Chapter 9 says the whole family should meet "upon the common ground of tolerance, understanding and love" (p. 122). - <2>Each other.</2> The book's only other "love and tolerance" is in Chapter 9. In A.A. everyone knows everyone else's troubles, which elsewhere might bring gossip, but "we almost invariably temper such talk by a spirit of love and tolerance" (p. 125). The next lines add a rule of thumb: don't tell another person's intimate experiences unless you're sure he'd approve (p. 125). - <3>Drinking and drinkers.</3> "We are careful never to show intolerance or hatred of drinking as an institution." (p. 103) A spirit of intolerance, the same page says, might drive away alcoholics whose lives could have been saved (p. 103). - <4>Other people's opinions.</4> "Real tolerance of other people's shortcomings and viewpoints" makes members more useful to others (p. 19), and newcomers at the early meetings Chapter 11 describes were won over partly by "the absence of intolerance of any kind" (p. 160).
98f37ac73331: Tolerance here isn't servility. On the page before the code, in the amends work, the book says: "As God's people we stand on our feet; we don't crawl before anyone." (p. 83)
1f562f1fa03e: Chapter 4 says a code alone didn't work for these men: "If a mere code of morals or a better philosophy of life were sufficient to overcome alcoholism, many of us would have recovered long ago." (p. 44) The code on page 84 comes after the inventory, the admission and the amends, inside a paragraph that asks God to remove the defects. The book doesn't link the two passages itself. But read in order, love and tolerance aren't offered as a way to get sober by effort alone. They're how the writers describe living once the work of Steps Four to Nine is under way.
9e0934b706b4: It confirms it. The line means what it says, and the chapter around it shows it as part of a daily practice that ends by turning to someone we can help.

0110cbee9e72: What the program text says protects sobriety most is something else: "nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics" (p. 89).
7b0d7c56b244: All our sources was searched for "meeting maker(s)," "make it" and "meeting," with page breaks joined. The saying isn't there. In the program text (pp. 1–164), the word "meeting" for an A.A. gathering appears only in Chapter 11 (pp. 159, 162). The other use in the program, "avoid meeting a man through his family" (p. 91), is about something else. Bill's "We meet frequently" (p. 15) uses the verb.
26dd95eb99c9: What the program text says about meetings
ddd35d9ea799: <0>Why they meet.</0> Bill W., writing of the fellowship in "one western city and its environs" (p. 15): "We meet frequently so that newcomers may find the fellowship they seek." (pp. 15–16).
31f02ea25630: <0>How the first meeting started.</0> In Akron, besides casual evenings in members' homes, "it became customary to set apart one night a week for a meeting" (p. 159). "Aside from fellowship and sociability, the prime object was to provide a time and place where new people might bring their problems." (p. 160).
9da6663f5eca: <0>What happened there.</0> Many a man still dazed from the hospital "has stepped over the threshold of that home into freedom" (p. 160). Already impressed by the members who had visited him in the hospital, he "capitulated entirely" when, in an upper room of the house, he heard a man tell a story that closely matched his own (p. 160). By 1939 the house was drawing sixty or eighty visitors a week (p. 161). The chapter gives the meeting real weight in a newcomer's turning point, alongside the hospital visits that came before it.
de50d15162d1: <0>More than meetings.</0> The same chapter: "But life among Alcoholics Anonymous is more than attending gatherings and visiting hospitals." (p. 161). It goes on to cleaning up old scrapes, settling family differences, lending money and finding jobs for each other (p. 161).
e468f28b94c5: <0>Travellers.</0> "Those of us who travel drop in as often as we can." (p. 162). The book gives two reasons: it lets them lend a hand, and it helps them avoid "certain alluring distractions of the road" (p. 162). That is the one place the program text links going to A.A. gatherings with a member's own protection, and it puts lending a hand first.
ec6fc81b9a20: Chapter 7, "Working With Others," which tells a member how to help a newcomer, doesn't mention meetings at all. It tells the member to tell the newcomer about the Fellowship and lend him the book on the first visit (p. 94). See: <0>Does the Big Book say "90 meetings in 90 days"?</0>
4f507304535f: What the program text says keeps a member sober
b7d886f1de14: The program text is direct about this, and it isn't attendance:
ad25a19d83bf: Chapter 7 opens by saying practical experience shows that "nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics" (p. 89).
dde2b2860d24: Bill: when all other measures failed, "work with another alcoholic would save the day" (p. 15).
de5592c2950d: And beneath that, a spiritual condition kept up daily: "What we really have is a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition." (p. 85).
a3b667167b93: An early warning about missing meetings
fedcc556222f: "The Back-Slider," a story printed in the 1939 first edition and dropped later, describes a man two years sober who decided it wouldn't hurt if he "carried on and missed a meeting or two" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003). Then "I began to neglect my daily communication with God" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003), and from there it was a short step to drinking. <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980) has an early Akron member, J. D., remember Dr. Bob saying one night that they should go and see a man who "had missed a meeting or two, and was just about ripe for a slip" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

c10135c3e89b: Meetings are in the early program as a place for newcomers to find fellowship and bring their problems, and Chapter 11 shows newcomers finding their answer there (p. 160). 030bdf08af8b: Is what I say at a meeting kept private?
27dfa4343dda: A.A.'s literature asks members to keep each other's confidences, but it describes a principle and a custom, not an enforceable rule. Today's group pamphlet: "We repeat no one's personal sharing made in A.A. meetings." (P-16, 2018). It calls the word "anonymous" in A.A.'s name "a promise of privacy" (P-16, 2018).
771b0fbd5ac6: The 1939 text's version is about the family of A.A.: "we do not relate intimate experiences of another person unless we are sure he would approve" (p. 125).
07a851702238: In 1946 Bill W. wrote that a newcomer's wish for privacy should be respected, even to the point of not discussing his case with other A.A. members (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946).
537991dc277d: The Traditions speak of anonymity at the public level (press, radio, films) and as a spiritual principle (pp. 562, 565–566); they don't address what is said inside a meeting. No A.A. text in our sources claims any legal protection for what is said at a meeting, and A.A. has no way to compel anyone.
cab08ed36ee1: The Big Book has no chapter on meeting confidentiality; it describes no meeting format at all. What it says about other people's stories is in Chapter 9, "The Family Afterward": - "We families of Alcoholics Anonymous keep few skeletons in the closet." (p. 125). Everyone knew about each other's alcoholic troubles. The book admits this would cause gossip in ordinary life; among them, it says, such things are rare, and talk is tempered "by a spirit of love and tolerance" (p. 125). - "Another principle we observe carefully is that we do not relate intimate experiences of another person unless we are sure he would approve." (p. 125). "We find it better, when possible, to stick to our own stories." (p. 125).
7537fda92535: Two other passages bear on keeping confidences: - The Fifth Step should be taken with someone "close-mouthed" (p. 74), and "It is important that he be able to keep a confidence" (p. 74). - An employer helping an alcoholic employee is asked to treat it as "a strictly personal matter" that will "never be discussed without his consent" (p. 143).
47e91fe4dc49: The 1939 Foreword's reasons for anonymity were practical: too few members to handle a flood of appeals, and business people who couldn't carry on their jobs if known (p. xiii).
c60e40195018: The Long Form's anonymity Traditions deal with the public: "Our names and pictures as A.A. members ought not be broadcast, filmed, or publicly printed." (p. 565). Tradition Twelve calls anonymity a spiritual principle that reminds members "to place principles before personalities" (p. 566). Neither speaks of what is said inside a meeting.
e4056b9175d2: Bill's 1946 essay "Anonymity" goes further on the personal level: - "It should be the privilege of each A.A. to cloak himself with as much personal anonymity as he desires." (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946). His fellow members should respect that. - Anonymity encourages alcoholics and their families to come for help, because they regard it "as an assurance their problems will be kept confidential" (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946). - "We ought, of course, to preserve a new member's anonymity so long as he wishes it preserved" (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946). "If he wishes us to refrain from discussing his case with anyone, even other A.A. members, we ought to respect that wish too." (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946).
670ee5c1cc84: He was also clear that anonymity isn't secrecy about oneself. Few members are anonymous in their daily contacts, he wrote in 1946, and in 1955: "Of course no A.A. need be anonymous to family, friends, or neighbors." (P-17, "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous", 1955). See <0>Tradition Twelve: does anonymity mean keeping A.A. secret?</0>
d72964547158: <0>The A.A. Group</0> (P-16): - At the personal level, anonymity "assures privacy for all members" (P-16, 2018), which matters especially to newcomers who fear their alcoholism may be exposed. - "We repeat no one's personal sharing made in A.A. meetings." (P-16, 2018). Members respect others' right to keep their anonymity "however they wish, and as closely as they wish" (P-16, 2018). - A chair may remind those present to "leave any confidences you hear in these rooms behind when you go" (P-16, 2018). 2b8e404a7589: When the Big Book came out in April 1939, A.A. had about a hundred members. The book's own foreword says "more than one hundred men and women" (p. xiii).
bb60c170c536: They were mostly in two places: Akron, Ohio (with Cleveland nearby) and New York, plus a few scattered "twos and threes and fives" elsewhere (p. 162).

d046b6e6b602: <0>Foreword to the First Edition.</0> Its first sentence says the members of Alcoholics Anonymous "are more than one hundred men and women who have recovered from a seemingly hopeless state of mind and body" (p. xiii). By 1939 the weekly meeting at a member's home drew "sixty or eighty as a rule," counting families who drove in from nearby towns (p. 161). - A community thirty miles away "has fifteen fellows of Alcoholics Anonymous" (p. 161). - In an eastern city (New York) there were informal meetings "where you may now see scores of members" (p. 162). - Elsewhere, "Little clusters of twos and threes and fives of us have sprung up in other communities" (p. 162).

94c1c340b6a6: <0>Foreword to the Second Edition (1955).</0> "The membership had then reached about 100 men and women." (p. xvii). It adds that in late 1937 enough members had lasting sobriety to convince them their way worked (p. xvii).

ce3840b4aeae: Should I give a newcomer money or a place to stay?
e05322cd7504: The Big Book says you may: if he's broke and homeless, help him find a job, give him "a little financial assistance," or take him into your home "for a few days" (p. 96).
38f29398a62f: It sets limits. Don't take money your family or creditors should have, make sure your family will welcome him, and make sure he isn't using you for money or shelter, because then "you only harm him" (p. 96). Members seldom let an alcoholic live with them for long (p. 97).
0f43383ad619: Money and shelter aren't the cure. Men who demand them "before conquering alcohol, are on the wrong track" (p. 98). The question is "when and how to give" (p. 98).
594d3de6ac5c: There's no yes-or-no rule in the text. It leaves this to judgment, and tells you to make sure you're doing the right thing before you take it on (p. 97).
1ab5dd537e26: <0>If all he wants is money or nursing.</0> If he expects you to act only as "a banker for his financial difficulties or a nurse for his sprees," you may have to drop him until he changes his mind (p. 95).
80842d82fea5: <0>If he's sincere and in need.</0> "He may be broke and homeless. If he is, you might try to help him about getting a job, or give him a little financial assistance" (p. 96). Not at your family's or creditors' expense (p. 96).
a206b14d3d8e: <0>Taking him in.</0> "Perhaps you will want to take the man into your home for a few days. But be sure you use discretion" (p. 96). Be certain your family welcomes him and that he isn't trying to impose on you "for money, connections, or shelter" (p. 96). If you allow that, you make it possible for him to be insincere, and "You may be aiding in his destruction rather than his recovery" (p. 97).
c8dc75cbafdb: <0>Don't dodge it, either.</0> "Never avoid these responsibilities, but be sure you are doing the right thing if you assume them" (p. 97). The work "may mean sharing your money and your home" (p. 97).
76abdb75c69c: <0>Not for long.</0> "We seldom allow an alcoholic to live in our homes for long at a time" (p. 97). It isn't good for him, and it can cause serious trouble in a family (p. 97).
0b6814e8a49a: <0>Why it isn't the main thing.</0> For the alcoholic who is able and willing to get well, "little charity, in the ordinary sense of the word, is needed or wanted" (pp. 97–98). Members still go to great lengths to provide each other these things "when such action is warranted" (p. 98). The minute the work becomes a service of handouts, the alcoholic starts relying on the helpers instead of on God (p. 98). "Burn the idea into the consciousness of every man that he can get well regardless of anyone" (p. 98).
08aecd0d814e: Chapter 11 says the early Akron members "shared their homes, their slender resources," and were willing day or night to put a new man in hospital and visit him (p. 159). In 1939, "lending money and securing jobs for each other, when justified" was an everyday thing (p. 161).

7048f1c6ff18: "There are no musts in A.A." isn't in the Big Book. In our sources it appears once, in <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980), as a one-line gloss on something Dr. Bob wrote in 1948.
0aaf0cbcbd9d: The 1939 program text uses "must" more than sixty times in Chapters 1 to 11, most often as "we must." Examples: "We must, or it kills us!" (p. 62), and "We must be entirely honest with somebody" (p. 73).
7d476cc4d3b4: The book is just as clear that no one should order anyone to follow it. The Steps are "suggested" (p. 59), the writers lay down "no rule of any sort" (p. 81), and "it is best that no one tell him he must abide by its suggestions" (p. 144).
a6835094c45d: So both halves are true. No one in A.A. can make you do anything. The book still says, from its writers' experience, that some things must be done if you want to recover.
2482f901233b: All our sources was searched for "no musts," "musts," "you must" and "Thou shalt not."
690483383f42: The only "no musts" is in <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980). It quotes Dr. Bob's article in the Grapevine of September 1948 about the Twelve Steps: - The Steps are "simple in language, plain in meaning" and workable by anyone with a sincere desire for sobriety (<1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1>, 1980). - "Yet, withal, there are no shibboleths in A.A." (<2>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</2>, 1980). Members aren't bound by theological doctrine, and "an A.A. decalogue in the language of 'Thou shalt not' would gall us indeed" (<3>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</3>, 1980).
b12ea86e4f51: The 1980 book then adds, in quotation marks: "That is, 'There are no musts in A.A.'" (<0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0>, 1980). The book doesn't say who first said it. The words quoted from 1948 are Dr. Bob's. The short form is the 1980 book's gloss.
28acbf68fdf8: The same article, quoted just before, also says that harmonious living comes in proportion to "our earnest attempt to follow them literally under divine guidance" (<0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0>, 1980). So Dr. Bob rejected an enforced code of "Thou shalt not." He didn't say the Steps were optional extras.
3d7e2312324b: (The question list said the "no musts" line sits next to a Bill W. passage. The passage is Dr. Bob's, from his 1948 Grapevine article.)
8e5c2d59c30e: The same 1980 book also uses "musts" the other way, about early Akron. Besides hospitalization and surrender, it says, "there were undoubtedly other musts, even though Dr. Bob and Bill weren't quite sure what they were" (<0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0>, 1980). Reading a 1938 report on the Akron group, it notes that members then thought meetings "desirable" but not necessary, while "Morning devotion and 'quiet time,' however, were musts" (<1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1>, 1980). So the book that prints the "no musts" gloss also records that the first members held some things to be musts for themselves. What Dr. Bob turned down in 1948 was a decalogue of "Thou shalt not" laid on members.
239e8a7366f6: <0>The writers took "you must" out on purpose.</0> Bill tells in <1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> (1957) that a psychiatrist who read the draft sent out before publication, Dr. Howard, said the text "was too full of the words 'you' and 'must'" (<2>A.A. Comes of Age</2>, 1957). He suggested changing them where possible to "we ought" or "we should," to remove all coercion. Bill gave in: "it was perfectly apparent that the doctor was dead right" (<3>A.A. Comes of Age</3>, 1957).
6947beb4ea9b: <0>The commonest form left is "we must."</0> A count of the fourth-edition text of Chapters 1–11 finds "must" or "mustn't" about sixty-eight times. The most common form by far is "we must" (twenty-three times, six of them in a list of rules the book rejects, below), against seven "you must." Many of the musts that remain report what the writers found they had to do: - On selfishness: above everything, alcoholics must be rid of it. "We must, or it kills us!" (p. 62). - On the Fifth Step: "We must be entirely honest with somebody if we expect to live long or happily in this world" (pp. 73–74). - On amends: "We must not shrink at anything" (p. 79). "We must lose our fear of creditors" (p. 78). - On daily life: "Every day is a day when we must carry the vision of God's will into all of our activities" (p. 85). - On spiritual life: "we must find a spiritual basis of life—or else" (p. 44).
ab11e4e459e1: <0>Where the book refuses a "must."</0> Chapter 7 lists the musts other people had laid on alcoholics: "we must not go where liquor is served"; "we must shun friends who drink"; "we must not go into bars" (pp. 100–101). "Our experience shows that this is not necessarily so" (p. 101).
df74bba75ff4: <0>It never lets one person order another.</0> A man given the book should not be told "he must abide by its suggestions" (p. 144). "The man must decide for himself" (p. 144). The newcomer, after reading, "must decide for himself whether he wants to go on" (p. 95). A wife should "never tell him what he must do about his drinking" (p. 111). The Traditions say the same about membership: it should never depend "upon money or conformity" (p. 563).
f922316331da: <0>The Steps are suggested.</0> "Here are the steps we took, which are suggested as a program of recovery" (p. 59). Bill says the suggestion wording was added in the same last-minute compromise as "God as we understood Him": the Steps "were to be suggestions only" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957). On a hard question about amends at home, the writers say they wish "to lay down no rule of any sort" (p. 81).
f25583a5af2f: <0>But "suggested" isn't "unimportant."</0> The same pages report what happened when people skipped things. "Half measures availed us nothing" (p. 59). "If we skip this vital step, we may not overcome drinking" (p. 72).
0585e11bccea: "There are no musts in A.A." is fair about authority. No one in A.A. can order a member to do anything, and the book was deliberately rewritten to avoid "you must." It isn't fair about the content. The book's writers say, many times and in their own voice, that certain things <0>must</0> be done: honesty, getting rid of selfishness, amends, daily reliance on God, helping others. It presents them as what they found necessary to stay alive, offered to anyone who wants what they have (p. 58).
79e4aafc7144: It's sometimes said there are no "musts" or requirements for A.A. membership or for sobriety. The membership half is right (Long Form Three, p. 563). The sobriety half goes beyond the book, which does name what its writers found they must do.

70972bd78990: What does "no outside affiliation" mean in practice?
03be5ccd6a2c: It means an A.A. group may cooperate with anyone, but never so far as "affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied." "An A.A. group can bind itself to no one" (p. 564).
d3b55015beff: A group is an A.A. group only if, as a group, it has "no other affiliation" (p. 563). It doesn't go into business, lend A.A.'s name to any facility or cause, take money with strings, or take sides on outside controversies.
d8057a63afc4: It limits A.A. groups and A.A. as a whole. In 1947 Bill W. wrote that individual members are free to work in hospitals, research or education, as individuals, so long as they keep A.A.'s name out of it.
272728159549: In practice it was learned from failures: groups that ran drying-out places and "A.A. hospitals," and members who tied A.A.'s name to causes.
8f383c2d25ae: <0>Tradition Three: what a group is.</0> Any two or three alcoholics gathered for sobriety may call themselves an A.A. group, "provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation" (p. 563).
e33269356306: <0>Tradition Six: how far cooperation goes.</0> Problems of money, property and authority "may easily divert us from our primary spiritual aim" (p. 563). So: - Any considerable property useful to A.A. should be separately incorporated, dividing the material from the spiritual (pp. 563–564). - "An A.A. group, as such, should never go into business" (p. 564). - Clubs and hospitals should be set apart so the groups can drop them if necessary, and shouldn't use the A.A. name (p. 564). - Hospitals and places of recuperation "ought to be well outside A.A. — and medically supervised" (p. 564). - "While an A.A. group may cooperate with anyone, such cooperation ought never go so far as affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied" (p. 564).
7fd90c06ebe3: <0>Tradition Seven: no strings.</0> No contributions "carrying any obligation whatever" (p. 564), and no public fund-raising in A.A.'s name, whether by groups, clubs, hospitals or outside agencies (p. 564).
bc1c87e985bb: <0>Tradition Ten: no sides.</0> "The Alcoholics Anonymous groups oppose no one" (p. 565).
d1bafb5b778f: What it looked like in practice (Bill W., 1946–47)
b9a538c227c0: <0>Groups running hospitals failed.</0> Where groups set up their own drying-out places with hired managers and nurses, it almost always backfired: "It has put the group into business" (P-17, "Hospitals and A.A.", 1947, p. 15). Groups that raised money publicly for "A.A. hospitals" got nowhere, because solicitation carrying A.A.'s endorsement is dangerous to everyone (P-17, pp. 15–16). What worked were rest farms run by individual members under medical supervision: "Not being a group project and not bearing the A.A. name," they could be taken or left alone (P-17, "Hospitals and A.A.", 1947, p. 16).
d3229f95c90b: <0>Cooperation is normal.</0> "Everywhere we cooperate with hospitals" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 33). Hospitals gave A.A. working arrangements, consulted it and employed A.A. nurses, and these relationships worked well, but none of these places were known as A.A. hospitals (P-17, p. 33).
f16cc102b667: <0>The line for groups.</0> "Neither A.A. as a whole nor any A.A. group ought to enter any activity other than straight A.A." (P-17, "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects", 1947, p. 24). Groups can't endorse, finance or ally with any other cause, however good, or link A.A.'s name to other alcohol work so that the public thinks A.A. has given up its own aim (P-17, p. 24). Members and friends in those fields should be discouraged from stressing A.A.'s name in publicity or fund-raising (P-17, pp. 24–25).
1186a1f365cf: <0>The freedom for members.</0> Bill calls the "do nothing" view unthinkable (P-17, p. 25). Members can bring their experience to other noncontroversial alcohol work if they act as individuals: no A.A. label in public and no use of A.A. status to raise money (P-17, p. 25). His summary: "A.A. does not sponsor projects in other fields" (P-17, "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects", 1947, p. 25), but members may work in constructive ones as individuals, careful of A.A.'s name (P-17, pp. 25–26).
b64559aa8a3e: Bill's 1955 foreword asks A.A. to "steadfastly decline all political, sectarian, or other alliances" (P-17, Foreword, 1955, p. 4). The 1955 essay on anonymity puts it plainly: A.A. will cooperate with almost everybody, "yet we decline to marry our Society to anyone" (P-17, "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous", 1955, p. 50). P-17 also prints a General Service Conference statement, undated, that A.A. follows a policy of cooperation but not affiliation with other organizations concerned with alcoholism (P-17, p. 36).
f82273ba39e5: It doesn't mean groups can't meet in churches, hospitals or treatment centres (a later pamphlet describes such groups as renting space there; P-16, 2018, pp. 17–18), or that A.A. can't work alongside hospitals and doctors; all of that is cooperation. It doesn't stop individual members working in other fields as individuals, provided they keep A.A.'s name out of it, and it doesn't bind outside organizations. What it rules out is a group, or A.A., belonging to, endorsing, financing, or lending its name to anything outside A.A.
